# Cardiac physiology

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Cardiology and angiology > Basics of cardiology > Cardiac physiology*

[Original Article Link](/library/zo0reS)

---

## Summary

The <u>heart</u> pumps blood through the <u>circulatory system</u> and supplies the body with blood. Cardiac activity can be assessed with measurable parameters, including <u>heart rate</u>, <u>stroke volume</u>, and <u>cardiac output</u>. The <u>cardiac cycle</u> consists of two phases: <u>systole</u>, in which blood is pumped from the <u>heart</u>, and <u>diastole</u>, in which the <u>heart</u> fills with blood. The <u>conduction system</u> is made up of a collection of nodes and specialized conduction cells that initiate and coordinate the contraction of the <u>myocardium</u>. Pacemaker cells (e.g., sinus node) of the <u>conduction system of the heart</u> autonomously and spontaneously generate an <u>action potential</u> (AP). The <u>conduction system</u> transmits the AP throughout the <u>myocardium</u>, and the electrical excitation of the <u>myocardium</u> results in its contraction. A phase of relaxation (<u>refractory period</u>) prevents immediate reexcitation. The <u>Frank-Starling mechanism</u> maintains <u>cardiac output</u> by increasing <u>myocardial contractility</u> and thus <u>stroke volume</u>, in response to an increased <u>preload</u> (<u>end-diastolic volume</u>). The <u>autonomic nervous system</u> is able to regulate the <u>heart rate</u> as well as cardiac excitability, conductivity, relaxation, and contractility.




![Action Potentials - Part 4: Myocardial Contractile Cells](media/small_60e31b109a1ae.jpg)

## Overview

The main function of the <u>heart</u> is to maintain blood circulation and ensure blood supply to the body through its continuous pumping action. The <u>heart</u>'s activity can be assessed using various parameters, including <u>heart rate</u>, <u>stroke volume</u>, and <u>cardiac output</u>.




### Definitions




* Heart rate (HR)

* The number of <u>heart</u> contractions per minute (bpm)

* <u>Normal heart rate at rest</u>: 60–100 bpm

* Stroke volume (<u>SV</u>)

* Volume of blood pumped by the left or <u>right ventricle</u> in a single heartbeat

* <u>SV</u> = end-diastolic volume (<u>EDV</u>) − end-systolic volume (<u>ESV</u>)

* Ejection fraction (EF): the <u>proportion</u> of <u>EDV</u> ejected from the ventricle

* EF = <u>SV</u> / <u>EDV</u> = (<u>EDV</u> - <u>ESV</u>)/<u>EDV</u>

* Normally 50–70%

* Serves as an index of myocardial contractility: e.g., ↓ <u>myocardial</u> contractility → ↓ EF (seen in <u>systolic heart failure</u>, where EF is < 40%)

* Low in <u>systolic heart failure</u> and usually normal in <u>diastolic heart failure</u>

* Venous return: the rate at which blood flows back to the <u>heart</u>, which typically equals <u>cardiac output</u> (see also section on “<u>Preload</u>” below)

* Cardiac output: the volume of blood the <u>heart</u> pumps through the <u>circulatory system</u> per minute (∼ 5 L/min at rest)

* Cardiac output (CO) = <u>heart</u> rate (HR) × <u>stroke</u> volume (<u>SV</u>)

* During physical activity (when <u>SV</u> becomes constant), an increase in <u>cardiac output</u> is mediated by increasing <u>heart rate</u>.

* Measurement

* Via Fick principle

* <u>Cardiac output</u> is proportional to the quotient of the total body oxygen consumption and the difference in oxygen content of arterial blood and mixed venous blood.

* <u>Cardiac output</u> (CO) = oxygen consumption rate/arteriovenous oxygen difference = (O<sub>2</sub> consumption)/(arterial O<sub>2</sub>content - venous O<sub>2</sub> content)

* Via mean arterial pressure (<u>MAP</u>)

* <u>MAP</u> = cardiac output (CO) × total peripheral resistance (TPR)

* Mean arterial pressure (<u>MAP</u>) = ⅓ systolic blood pressure (SP) + ⅔ <u>diastolic</u> blood pressure (DP) = (SP + 2 x DP)/3

* As HR increases, <u>diastole</u> is shortened, which decreases <u>SV</u> due to less filling time.

* Increase in CO is achieved through a significant increase in HR and a slight increase in <u>SV</u>.

* The increased HR shortens the filling time (<u>diastole</u>), which limits the increase in <u>SV</u>.

* As the HR reaches ≥ 160/bpm, maximum CO is reached and begins to decrease, as <u>SV</u> declines faster than HR increases.

* During exercise, a healthy young adult can increase their CO by a factor of approx. 4–5 the resting rate of 5 L/min, i.e., to approx. 20–25 L/min.

* Cardiac index: <u>cardiac output</u> (L/min) in relation to body surface area (m<sup>2</sup>)

* Volumetric flow rate

* Volume of blood that flows across a valve per second

* Volumetric flow rate (Q) = average flow <u>velocity</u> (v) × cross-sectional area occupied by the blood (A) 

* Amount of fluid entering the system must equal the amount leaving the system: Since Q<sub>1</sub> = Q<sub>2</sub>,A<sub>1</sub>v<sub>1</sub>= A<sub>2</sub>v<sub>2</sub> (discharge at section 1 = discharge at section 2)

* Used to calculate flow across stenotic valves, vessels of different diameters, etc.

* Myocardial oxygen demand

* Amount of oxygen required for optimal <u>heart</u> function

* Depends mainly on four factors:

* <u>Heart rate</u>

* Contractility

* Wall tension (ventricular diameter)

* <u>Afterload</u>

* <u>Coronary sinus</u>

* Receives drainage from most epicardial ventricular <u>veins</u>

* Contains majority of deoxygenated blood in the body

* Cardiac blood pressures (measured via <u>Swan-Ganz catheterization</u>)

* <u>Right atrium</u>: < 5 mm Hg

* <u>Right ventricle</u> (<u>pulmonary artery</u> pressure): 25/5 mm Hg

* <u>Left atrium</u> (<u>pulmonary capillary wedge pressure</u>): < 12 mm Hg (higher than <u>left ventricular</u> pressure in <u>mitral stenosis</u>)

* <u>Left ventricle</u>: 130/10 mm Hg

* Coronary perfusion pressure

* The driving pressure that forces blood into the <u>coronary arteries</u> during <u>diastole</u>

* Calculated as the difference in pressure between the aorta and <u>left ventricle</u> during <u>diastole</u>

---

## Cardiac cycle

The <u>cardiac cycle</u> can be divided into two phases: <u>systole</u>, in which blood is pumped from the <u>heart</u>, and <u>diastole</u>, in which the <u>heart</u> fills with blood. <u>Systole</u> and <u>diastole</u> are each subdivided into two further phases, resulting in a total of four phases of <u>heart</u> action. Depending on the phase, pressure and volume in the ventricles and <u>atria</u> change, with the pressure in the <u>left ventricle</u> changing the most and the pressure in the <u>atria</u> the least.




### Systole




#### 1.) Isovolumetric contraction




* Main function: ventricular contraction

* Follows <u>ventricular filling</u>

* Occurs in early <u>systole</u>, directly after the <u>atrioventricular valves</u> (<u>AV valves</u>) close and before the <u>semilunar valves</u> open (all valves are closed)

* Ventricle contracts (i.e., pressure increases) with no corresponding ventricular volume change

* LV pressure: 8 mm Hg → ∼ 80 mm Hg (when aortic and pulmonary valves open passively)

* LV volume: remains ∼ 150 mL

* RV pressure: 5 mm Hg → 25 mm Hg

* RV volume: ∼ 150 mL [[1]](/library/JHXsrz)

* The period of highest O<sub>2</sub> consumption





#### 2.) Systolic ejection




* Main function: Blood is pumped from the ventricles into the circulation and <u>lungs</u>.

* Follows <u>isovolumetric contraction</u>

* Occurs between the opening and closing of the <u>aortic valve</u> and <u>pulmonary valve</u>

* Ventricles contract (i.e., pressure increases) to eject blood, which decreases the ventricular volume

* Pressure: first increases from ∼ 80 mm Hg to 120 mm Hg and then decreases until aortic and pulmonary valves close

* Volume: ejection of ∼ 90 mL <u>SV</u> (150 mL → 60 mL)





### Diastole




#### 3.) Isovolumetric relaxation




* Main function: ventricular relaxation

* Follows <u>systolic ejection</u>

* Occurs between <u>aortic valve</u> closing and <u>mitral valve</u> opening

* All valves closed (volume remains constant)
* Dicrotic notch: slight increase of aortic pressure in the early <u>diastole</u> that corresponds to closure of the <u>aortic valve</u>

* The ventricles relax (i.e., pressure decreases) with no corresponding ventricular volume change until ventricular pressure is lower than atrial pressure and <u>atrioventricular valves</u> open

* Pressure: decreases to ∼ 10 mm Hg in the <u>left ventricle</u> and ∼ 5 mm Hg in the <u>right ventricle</u>

* Volume: remains at ∼ 60 mL

* Coronary blood flow peaks during early <u>diastole</u> at the point when the pressure differential between the aorta and the ventricle is the greatest.
* The <u>coronary arteries</u> fill with blood during <u>diastole</u> because they are compressed during ventricular <u>systole</u>.





#### 4.) Ventricular filling




Main function: ventricles fill with blood




##### Rapid filling




* Follows <u>isovolumetric relaxation</u>

* Occurs in early <u>diastole</u>; immediately after <u>mitral valve</u> opening

* Blood flows passively from the <u>atria</u> to the ventricles.

* The largest volume of <u>ventricular filling</u> occurs during this phase.





##### Reduced filling




* Follows rapid filling

* Occurs in late <u>diastole</u>; immediately before <u>atrioventricular valves</u> close

* LV pressure: ∼ 8 mm Hg; RV pressure: ∼ 5 mm Hg (2–8 mm Hg)

* LV and RV volume: ventricles fill with ∼ 90 mL (60 mL → 150 mL) [[2]](/library/qHXCrz)





> [!NOTE]
> During <u>isovolumetric contraction</u> and relaxation, all <u>heart valves</u> are closed. There are no periods in which all <u>heart valves</u> are open.




> [!NOTE]
> During states of increased <u>heart rate</u> (e.g., during exercise), the duration of <u>diastole</u> decreases so that there is less time for the <u>coronary arteries</u> to fill with blood and supply the <u>heart</u> with oxygen. Patients with narrow <u>coronary arteries</u>, e.g., due to <u>atherosclerosis</u>, will, therefore, experience <u>chest pain</u> (<u>angina pectoris</u>) during exertion.

### <u>Left ventricular</u> pressure-volume diagram




* Used to: measure cardiac performance

* Shape: roughly rectangular; each loop is formed in a counter-clockwise direction

* Course 

* (1) End-<u>diastolic</u> state: closure of the <u>atrioventricular valve</u> and the beginning of <u>systole</u> (the LV is filled with blood)

* (1 → 2) <u>Isovolumetric contraction</u>: With the atrioventricular and <u>semilunar valves</u> closed, contraction increases the internal pressure of the <u>left ventricle</u>; ventricular volume is left unchanged.

* (2) Opening of the <u>semilunar valve</u> when the ventricular pressure exceeds the aortic and pulmonary arterial pressure

* (2 → 3) Ejection phase: The ventricle pumps out the <u>stroke volume</u>.

* (3) Closure of the <u>semilunar valve</u> when the ventricular pressure falls below the aortic and pulmonary arterial pressure

* (3 → 4) <u>Isovolumetric relaxation</u>: the beginning of <u>diastole</u>, when the ventricle relaxes and all the valves are closed

* (4) Opening of the <u>atrioventricular valve</u> when the ventricular pressure falls below the atrial pressure

* (4 → 1) <u>Filling phase</u>: The ventricles receive blood from the <u>atria</u> and a new <u>cardiac cycle</u> begins.

| Overview |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Valvular disease | <u>Pressure-volume loop</u> | Time-pressure curves |
| <u>Mitral regurgitation</u> | <br><br>* Rounder and flatter pressure-volume loop than normal.<br><br>* ↑ LV <u>end-diastolic volume</u> and pressure<br><br>* ↑ <u>Stroke volume</u><br><br>* No <u>isovolumetric contraction</u><br><br>* No <u>isovolumetric relaxation</u><br><br>* ↓ LV <u>end-systolic volume</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Tall <u>V-wave</u><br><br> |
| <u>Mitral stenosis</u> | <br><br>* The <u>pressure-volume loop</u> is narrower and flatter than the normal <u>pressure-volume loop</u>.<br><br>* ↑ LA pressure<br><br>* ↓ LV <u>end-diastolic volume</u><br><br>* ↓ <u>Stroke volume</u><br><br>* ↓ LV <u>end-systolic volume</u><br><br><br> | <br>* LA pressure > LV pressure during <u>diastole</u><br><br> |
| <u>Aortic regurgitation</u> | <br><br>* The <u>pressure-volume loop</u> is rounder and taller than the normal <u>pressure-volume loop</u>.<br><br>* ↑ LV <u>end-diastolic volume</u><br><br>* ↑ <u>Stroke volume</u><br><br>* Normal or ↑ LV <u>diastolic</u> pressure<br><br>* No true <u>isovolumetric relaxation</u><br><br><br> | <br>* ↑ <u>Pulse pressure</u><br><br> |
| <u>Aortic stenosis</u> | <br><br>* The <u>pressure-volume loop</u> is narrower and taller than the normal <u>pressure-volume loop</u>.<br><br>* ↑ LV end-systolic pressure<br><br>* No change in <u>end-diastolic volume</u><br><br>* ↓ <u>Stroke volume</u><br><br>* ↑ LV <u>end-systolic volume</u><br><br>* ↑ LV end-<u>diastolic</u> pressure<br><br><br> | <br>* LV blood pressure > aortic pressure during <u>systole</u><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> The width of the volume-pressure loop is the <u>SV</u> (the difference between <u>EDV</u> and <u>ESV</u>).

## Conduction system of the heart

Definition: the collection of nodes and specialized conduction cells that initiate and coordinate contraction of the <u>heart muscle</u>




| <br>Overview of the <u>conduction system of the heart</u> <br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Name | Anatomic localization | Characteristics | Frequency |
| Sinoatrial node | <br>* Upper wall of the <u>right atrium</u> (at the junction where the <u>SVC</u> enters)<br><br> | <br><br>* Natural pacemaker center of the <u>heart</u> with specialized pacemaker cells<br><br>* Spontaneously generates electrical impulses that initiate a heartbeat<br><br>* Influenced by <u>autonomic nervous system</u><br><br>* Transmits signals to the <u>left atrium</u> via interatrial bundle<br><br>* Supplied by sinus node <u>artery</u> (branch of the <u>right coronary artery</u>)<br><br><br> | <br>* ca. 60–80/min<br><br> |
| Atrioventricular node | <br>* Within the AV septum in the region known as the <u>Koch triangle</u>, superior and <u>medial</u> to the opening of the <u>coronary sinus</u> in the <u>right atrium</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Receives impulses from the <u>SA node</u> and passes these impulses to the <u>bundle of His</u><br><br>* Has the slowest conduction <u>velocity</u><br><br>* Delays conduction for 60–120 ms (allowing the ventricles to fill with blood; without this delay, the <u>atria</u> and ventricles would contract at the same time)<br><br>* Supplied by the <u>AV nodal</u> <u>artery</u> (<u>posterior descending artery</u> of <u>right coronary artery</u>)<br><br><br> | <br>* ca. 40–50/min<br><br> |
| Bundle of His | <br>* Directly below the <u>cardiac skeleton</u>, within the membranous part of the interventricular septum<br><br> | <br><br>* Receives impulses from the <u>AV node</u><br><br>* Splits into left and right bundle branches (<u>Tawara branches</u>) → the right bundle travels to the <u>right ventricle</u>; the left bundle splits into an <u>anterior</u> and a <u>posterior</u> branch to supply the left ventricle → terminate into terminal conducting fibers (<u>Purkinje fibers</u>) of the left and <u>right ventricle</u><br><br>* Prevents retrograde conduction<br><br>* Filters high-frequency <u>action potentials</u> so that high atrial rates (e.g., in <u>atrial fibrillation</u>) are not conducted to the <u>myocardium</u><br><br><br> | <br>* ca. 30–40/min<br><br> |
| <br><br>Purkinje fibers <br> | <br>* Terminal conducting fibers in the subendocardium<br><br> | <br><br>* Conduct cardiac AP faster than any other cardiac cells<br><br>* Ensure synchronized contraction of the ventricles<br><br>* <u>Purkinje fibers</u> have a long <u>refractory period</u>.<br><br>* Form functional syncytium: forward incoming stimuli very quickly via <u>gap junctions</u> to allow coordinated contraction<br><br><br> | <br>* ca. 30–40/min<br><br> |

### Normal course of electrical conduction




* <u>SA node</u> (pacemaker) creates an <u>action potential</u>.

* Signal spreads across <u>atria</u> and causes their contraction.

* Signal reaches <u>AV node</u> and is slowed down.

* <u>AV node</u> conducts the signal to <u>bundle of His</u> down the interventricular septum to <u>Purkinje fibers</u> in <u>myocardium</u>.

* <u>Purkinje fibers</u> carry the signal across the ventricles.

* The ventricles contract (<u>electromechanical coupling</u>).





> [!NOTE]
> The electrical activity of the <u>heart</u> can be recorded through <u>electrocardiography</u>. See <u>ECG</u> for an overview of <u>ECGs</u> and their interpretation.

## Heart excitation

### Overview




* Cardiac pacemaker cells (e.g., sinus node) of the <u>conduction system of the heart</u> autonomously and spontaneously generate an <u>action potential</u> (AP).

* The <u>conduction system</u> transmits the AP throughout the <u>myocardium</u>.

* The electrical excitation of the <u>myocardium</u> results in its contraction (see <u>electromechanical coupling</u> and filament sliding theory in <u>muscle tissue</u>).

* The phase of relaxation prevents immediate re-excitation (<u>refractory period</u>).

* <u>Gap junctions</u> are found in both pacemaker and contractile <u>myocardial cells</u> (not in <u>skeletal muscle</u> cells).





#### Cardiac <u>calcium</u> channels and <u>calcium</u> pumps




| Overview |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Name |  | Definition | Location | Direction of flow | Activation phase (affected tissue) |
| <u>Calcium</u> channels | <br>L-type voltage-gated calcium channel<br> | <br><br>* Long-acting, high-<u>voltage</u> channels that are responsible for <u>electromechanical coupling</u><br><br>* Activation via <u>depolarization</u> (- 40 mV) triggers <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> influx into the cells, which in turn stimulates the release of <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> from the SR.<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Cell membrane</u> of <u>cardiomyocytes</u><br><br> | <br>* Influx of extracellular <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> into the <u>cytoplasm</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Plateau phase (<u>myocardium</u>)<br><br>* Upstroke phase (<u>SA node</u>)<br><br><br> |
| T-type voltage-gated calcium channel | <br>* A <u>voltage-gated calcium channel</u> that is opened by low-<u>voltage</u> <u>depolarization</u> potentials<br><br> | <br>* <u>Cell membrane</u> of <u>cardiac pacemaker cells</u><br><br> | <br>* Influx of extracellular <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> into the <u>cytoplasm</u><br><br> | <br>* During the middle of phase 4 in pacemaker cells (<u>SA node</u>)<br><br> |  |
| <u>Ryanodine receptor</u> | <br>* <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> channel that opens after binding of <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> (i.e., <u>calcium</u>-induced <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> release)<br><br> | <br>* Membrane of SR<br><br> | <br>* Transport <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> from SR to the <u>cytoplasm</u><br><br> | <br>* Plateau phase (<u>myocardium</u>)<br><br> |  |
| <u>Calcium</u> pumps | <br>SERCA (sarcoplasmic <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u>-ATPase) | <br>* <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> pumps and exchangers that are responsible for terminating a contraction<br><br> | <br>* Membrane of SR<br><br> | <br>* Efflux of <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> from the <u>cytoplasm</u> into the SR<br><br> | <br>* Plateau phase (<u>myocardium</u>)<br><br> |
| Na+/Ca2+ exchanger | <br>* <u>Cell membrane</u> of <u>cardiomyocytes</u><br><br> | <br>* Efflux of <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> from the <u>cytoplasm</u> into <u>extracellular space</u><br><br> |  |  |  |





> [!NOTE]
> The long plateau phase of the <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> channels allows the <u>myocardium</u> to contract and pump blood effectively.




#### Other <u>cation</u> channels




All of these channels are located in <u>the cell</u> membrane.

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Name |  | Definition | Direction of flow | Activation phase (affected tissue) |
| <br>Funny channels (HCN, I<sub>f</sub>) |  | <br>* Nonselective <u>cation</u> channels (e.g., for Na<sup>+</sup>, <u>K<sup>+</sup></u>) in pacemaker cells that open as the membrane potential becomes more negative (hyperpolarized)<br><br> | <br>* Extracellular → intracellular<br><br> | <br>* Upstroke phase (sinus node)<br><br> |
| <br>Fast <u>sodium</u> channels (I<sub>Na</sub>) |  | <br>* Na<sup>+</sup> channels that rapidly open and close following <u>depolarization</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Depolarization</u> (<u>myocardium</u>)<br><br> |  |
| <u>Potassium</u> channels | Inward rectifier K<sup>+</sup> channels | <br>* <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> channels that open during the <u>resting potential</u> (below −70 mV) and stabilize the <u>resting potential</u> of the <u>cardiomyocytes</u><br><br> | <br>* Intracellular → extracellular<br><br> | <br>* <u>Resting potential</u> (primarily <u>myocardium</u>; sinus node)<br><br> |
| <br>Delayed rectifier K<sup>+</sup> channels(I<sub>Kr</sub> and I<sub>Ks</sub>) | <br>* <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> channels that can be rapidly (I<sub>Kr</sub>) or slowly (I<sub>Ks</sub>) activated upon <u>depolarization</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Repolarization</u> (sinus node and <u>myocardium</u>)<br><br> |  |  |





### <u>Cardiac action potential</u>




| Overview |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | <br>Myocardial action potential (<u>myocardium</u>, <u>bundle of His</u>, <u>Purkinje fibers</u>) | <br>Pacemaker action potential (<u>SA node</u> and <u>AV node</u>)<br> |
| <br>Phase 0  (upstroke and <u>depolarization</u>)<br> | <br><br>* Upstroke: An <u>action potential</u> from a pacemaker cell or adjacent <u>cardiomyocyte</u> causes the transmembrane potential (TMP) to rise above −90 mV.<br><br>* <u>Depolarization</u>: Fast <u>voltage-gated Na<sup>+</sup> channels</u> open at -65 mV → rapid Na<sup>+</sup> influx into <u>the cell</u> → TMP rises further until slightly above 0 mV<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Upstroke: At TMP -40 mV (<u>threshold potential</u> of pacemaker cells), L-type <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> channels open → TMP increases to +40 mV<br><br>* No rapid <u>depolarization</u> phase because fast <u>voltage-gated Na<sup>+</sup> channels</u> are inactivated in pacemaker cells  → results in slower conduction <u>velocity</u> between <u>atria</u> and ventricles<br><br><br> |
| <br>Phase 1 (early <u>repolarization</u>)<br> | <br><br>* Inactivation of <u>voltage-gated Na<sup>+</sup> channels</u><br><br>* Transient <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> channels start to open (outward flow of <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> returns TMP to 0 mV)<br><br><br> | <br>* Absent<br><br> |
| <br>Phase 2 (plateau phase)<br> | <br><br>* <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> efﬂux through <u>delayed rectifier K<sup>+</sup> channels</u> and <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> inﬂux through <u>voltage</u>-gated <u>L-type Ca<sup>2+</sup>channels</u>, which triggers <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> release from the <u>sarcoplasmic reticulum</u> (i.e., <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u>-induced <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u>release) → contraction of the <u>myocyte</u><br><br>* Unlike skeletal <u>myocytes</u>, cardiac <u>myocytes</u> require an extracellular influx of <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> for <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> to be released from the SR.<br><br>* TMP is maintained at a plateau just below 0 mV.<br><br><br> | <br>* Absent<br><br> |
| <br>Phase 3 (rapid <u>repolarization</u>)<br> | <br><br>* Inactivation of <u>voltage-gated Ca<sup>2+</sup> channels</u><br><br>* <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> efﬂux through delayed rectifier <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> channels continues: Persistent outflow of <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> exceeds <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> inflow and brings TMP back to -90 mV.<br><br>* The <u>sarcolemmal</u> <u>Na<sup>+</sup>-Ca<sup>2+</sup> exchanger</u>, <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u>-ATPase, and <u>Na<sup>+</sup>-K<sup>+</sup>-ATPase</u> restore normal transmembrane ionic concentration gradients (Na<sup>+</sup> and <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> ions return to <u>extracellular space</u>, <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> to <u>intracellular space</u>).<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Closure of <u>voltage</u>-gated <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> channels and<br><br>* Opening of delayed rectifier <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> channels → <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> efﬂux (TMP returns to -60 mV)<br><br><br> |
| <br>Phase 4 (<u>resting phase</u>)<br> | <br><br>* <u>Resting membrane potential</u> stable at -90 mV due to a constant outward flow of <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> through inward rectifier channels<br><br>* Na<sup>+</sup> and <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> channels closed<br><br><br> | <br><br>* No <u>resting phase</u> (unstable membrane potential)<br>* Gradual Na<sup>+</sup>/<u>K<sup>+</sup></u> entry via <u>funny channels</u> I<sub>f</sub> (<u>funny current</u> or pacemaker current) → slow spontaneous <u>depolarization</u> (TMP raises above -60 mV); no external <u>action potential</u> needed (automaticity of SA and <u>AV nodes</u>)<br>* At TMP -50 mV: T-type <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> channels open.<br><br>* <u>Sympathetic</u> stimulation → ↑ I<sub>f</sub> channels conductance → ↑ slope of phase 4 → ↑ <u>heart rate</u><br><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> Pacemaker cells have no stable <u>resting membrane potential</u>. Their special <u>hyperpolarization</u>-activated <u>cation</u> channels (<u>funny channels</u>) ensure a spontaneous new <u>depolarization</u> at the end of each <u>repolarization</u> and are responsible for the <u>automaticity of the heart</u> <u>conduction system</u>. In <u>sympathetic</u> stimulation, more I<sub>f</sub> channels open, increasing the <u>heart rate</u>.




> [!NOTE]
> Upstroke and <u>depolarization</u> of a pacemaker cell are caused by the opening of <u>voltage</u>-activated <u>L-type calcium channels</u>. In other muscle cells and <u>neurons</u>, upstroke and <u>depolarization</u> are caused by fast <u>sodium</u> channels.




> [!NOTE]
> The duration of <u>action potentials</u> differs in the various structures of the <u>conduction system</u> and increases from the sinus node to the <u>Purkinje fibers</u>.

### <u>Refractory period</u>




* Effective refractory period (<u>ERP</u>)

* Recovery period immediately after stimulation, during which a second stimulus cannot generate a new AP in a depolarized <u>cardiomyocyte</u>.

* Na<sup>+</sup> channels are in an inactivated state until <u>the cell</u> fully <u>repolarizes</u> (phases 1–3).

* See “<u>Refractory period</u>” for details.

* Phases (determined based on the number of <u>sodium</u> channels ready to be reactivated)

* Absolute refractory period: time interval in which no new AP can be generated because fast Na<sup>+</sup> channels are deactivated (plateau phase)

* Relative refractory period: time interval in which some Na+ channels can be reactivated but have a higher <u>threshold potential</u>; only a strong impulse can trigger a new, low amplitude AP

* Supernormal period: period of supernormal excitability of the <u>myocardium</u> during <u>repolarization</u> (some parts of the <u>heart</u> are excited and others unexcited)

* Effect

* Ensures sufficient time for chamber emptying (during <u>systole</u>) and refilling (during <u>diastole</u>) before the next contraction

* Prevents re-excitation of <u>cardiomyocytes</u> during this period to avoid circulatory excitation, which would lead to <u>arrhythmia</u> and <u>tetany</u> of <u>cardiac muscle</u>





> [!NOTE]
> The firing frequency of the <u>SA node</u> is faster than that of other pacemaker sites (e.g., <u>AV node</u>). The <u>SA node</u> activates these sites before they can activate themselves (overdrive suppression).




> [!NOTE]
> The plateau phase of the <u>myocardial action potential</u> is longer than the actual contraction. This allows the <u>heart muscle</u> to relax after each contraction and prevents permanent contraction (<u>tetany</u>).




> [!NOTE]
> Heterogeneity of the <u>refractory period</u> within the <u>myocardium</u> (in which some cells are in the <u>absolute refractory period</u>, <u>relative refractory period</u>, or <u>resting potential</u> state) renders individuals more susceptible to <u>arrhythmias</u> (e.g., <u>ventricular fibrillation</u>) when exposed to an inappropriately-timed stimulus.




> [!NOTE]
> During <u>cardioversion</u>, <u>shock</u> delivery must be synchronized with the R wave on <u>ECG</u> (indicating <u>depolarization</u>) and avoided during the <u>relative refractory period</u> (<u>T waves</u>, indicating <u>repolarization</u>).

## Regulation of cardiac activity

Adaptation to short-term changes is provided by the <u>Frank-Starling mechanism</u>. Long-term changes in cardiac activity are regulated by the <u>autonomic nervous system</u>.




### Frank-Starling mechanism




* Definition: a law that describes the relationship between <u>end-diastolic volume</u> and cardiac <u>stroke volume</u>
* Cardiac contractility is directly related to the wall tension of the <u>myocardium</u>.

* An increase in <u>end-diastolic volume</u> (<u>preload</u>) will cause the <u>myocardium</u> to stretch (↑ end-<u>diastolic</u> length of <u>cardiac muscle</u> fibers), which increases contractility (↑ force of contraction) and results in increased <u>stroke volume</u> in order to maintain <u>cardiac output</u>.

* This relationship between <u>end-diastolic volume</u> and <u>stroke volume</u> is shown in the <u>Frank-Starling curve</u>.

* Aim: maintain CO by modulating contractility and <u>SV</u>
* <u>Stroke volume</u> of both ventricles should remain the same.





> [!NOTE]
> Because the <u>afterload</u> is chronically increased in chronic <u>hypertension</u>, the <u>left ventricle</u> undergoes <u>hypertrophy</u> to decrease <u>left ventricular</u> wall <u>stress</u> (↑ LV wall thickness → ↓ LV wall <u>stress</u>).




> [!NOTE]
> An increase in <u>preload</u> leads to an increase in <u>stroke volume</u>; an increase in <u>afterload</u> leads to a decrease in <u>stroke volume</u>.

### Autonomic innervation of the <u>heart</u>




#### Overview




* The <u>autonomic nervous system</u> is able to regulate <u>heart rate</u>, excitability, conductivity, relaxation, and contractility.

* <u>Sympathetic</u> fibers innervate both the <u>atria</u> and ventricles. <u>Parasympathetic</u> fibers only innervate the <u>atria</u>.

* Modulation of cardiac action by <u>sympathetic</u> and/or <u>parasympathetic</u> nerve fibers

* Function: long-term regulation of cardiac action





#### Definitions




* Chronotropy: any influence on the <u>heart rate</u>

* Dromotropy: any influence on the conductivity of <u>myocardium</u>

* Inotropy: any influence on the force of <u>myocardial</u> contraction

* Lusitropy: any influence on the rate of relaxation of the <u>myocardium</u>

* Bathmotropy: any influence on the excitability of the <u>myocardium</u>





| Overview of autonomic innervation of the heart |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Site of innervation | Nerves | Effect | Mechanism of action |
| <br><u>Sympathetic</u> stimulation  <br> | <br>* <u>Atria</u> and ventricles<br><br> | <br>* Fibers from the <u>sympathetic</u> cervical trunk  (superior, middle, and inferior cardiac nerve)<br><br> | <br>* ↑ <u>Heart rate</u>, conduction, contractility, and relaxation<br><br> | <br>* Activation of beta<sub>1</sub> <u>adrenergic receptors</u> (<u>G<sub>s</sub>protein</u>-coupled) of the <u>heart</u> by <u>epinephrine</u> and <u>norepinephrine</u> → ↑ activity of <u>adenylyl cyclase</u> → ↑ intracellular <u>cAMP</u> concentration in <u>SA node</u> <u>cardiomyocytes</u>, which then:<br>1. * Increases the conductance of funny <u>sodium</u> channels and L-type <u>calcium</u> channels → ↑ influx of <u>cations</u> during spontaneous <u>depolarization</u> → faster attainment of the <u>threshold potential</u> during phase 4 of <u>pacemaker action potential</u> for initiating the rhythmic <u>cardiac action potential</u> → ↑ <u>heart rate</u> (positive <u>chronotropic</u>)<br>2. * Activates <u>protein kinase A</u> (<u>PKA</u>), which leads to two effects:<br><br>* <u>Phosphorylation</u> of <u>L-type Ca<sup>2+</sup> channels</u> in <u>AV node</u> → ↑ <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> entry → ↑ <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u>-induced <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> release during <u>action potential</u> → ↑ contraction and conduction (positive <u>inotropic</u> and <u>dromotropic</u>)<br><br>* <u>Phosphorylation</u> of phospholamban (a protein expressed in <u>cardiomyocytes</u> that decreases the affinity of <u>sarcoplasmic reticulum</u> <u>calcium</u>-ATPase for <u>calcium</u>)  → activation of <u>sarcoplasmic reticulum</u> <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u>-ATPase (<u>SERCA</u>) → ↑ transport of <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> back into <u>sarcoplasmic reticulum</u> after a contraction → faster relaxation (positive <u>lusitropic</u>)<br><br> |
| <br><u>Parasympathetic</u> stimulation (e.g., stimulation of the <u>cervix</u> or the urinary and anal sphincters) | <br>* <u>Atria</u><br><br> | <br>* Branches of the <u>vagus nerve</u> <br><br>* Cervical cardiac branches<br><br>* Thoracic cardiac branches<br><br> | <br>* ↓ <u>Heart rate</u> and atrial contractility<br><br> | <br>* Exerts its action on the <u>heart</u> through <u>parasympathetic</u> <u>muscarinic ACh receptors</u> (subtype M2) on SA and <u>AV node</u> <u>cardiomyocytes</u><br><br>* Activation of M<sub>2</sub> <u>receptors</u> on <u>SA node</u> (negative <u>chronotropic</u>)<br><br>* Reduces the conductance of funny <u>sodium</u> channels via <u>adenylyl cyclase</u>, decreasing <u>cAMP</u> → ↓ pacemaker current (lengthens the rate of <u>depolarization</u> in the slow <u>depolarization</u> phase)<br><br>* Increases conductance of the slow <u>potassium</u> channels → <u>hyperpolarization</u> of the <u>resting membrane potential</u> (harder to overcome)<br><br>* <u>Vagal</u> fibers innervate the <u>AV node</u> (negative <u>dromotropic</u>): slows <u>cardiac action potential</u> propagation (can result in <u>complete AV block</u>)<br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> Persistent <u>epinephrine</u> surges and long-lasting <u>sympathetic</u> activity can damage blood vessel <u>endothelium</u>, increase blood pressure, and increase the risk of <u>heart attack</u> and <u>stroke</u>.




> [!NOTE]
> Initially, a diminished <u>ejection fraction</u> can be compensated by increased <u>sympathetic</u> tone, <u>RAAS</u> activation, <u>ADH</u> release, and the <u>Frank-Starling mechanism</u>. In the long term, however, these mechanisms increase cardiac work and lead to <u>heart failure</u>. <u>Antihypertensive drugs</u> target these mechanisms.

## Factors that affect cardiac output

* Preload: the extent to which <u>heart muscle</u> fibers are stretched before the onset of <u>systole</u>; depends on <u>end-diastolic ventricular volume</u> (<u>EDV</u>), which changes according to:

* Venous constriction: ↑ venous tone → ↑ venous blood return to the <u>heart</u> → ↑ <u>EDV</u> → ↑ <u>preload</u>

* Circulating blood volume: ↑ circulating blood volume → ↑ venous blood return to the <u>heart</u> → ↑ <u>EDV</u> → ↑ <u>preload</u>

* Afterload: the force against which the ventricle contracts to eject blood during <u>systole</u>

* <u>Afterload</u> is primarily determined by the <u>mean arterial pressure</u> (<u>MAP</u>) in the aorta, which is influenced by <u>total peripheral resistance</u>.

* ↑ <u>Afterload</u> → ↑ <u>left ventricular</u> pressure → ↑ <u>left ventricular</u> wall <u>stress</u>

* According to <u>Laplace's law</u>, ↑ <u>left ventricular</u> pressure → ↑ <u>left ventricular</u> wall <u>stress</u>
* <u>Left ventricular</u> (LV) wall <u>stress</u> = (LV pressure × radius)/ (2×LV wall thickness)





| <br>Overview of <u>factors that affect cardiac output</u> <br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Factors that increase <u>SV</u> | Factors that decrease <u>SV</u> |
| <br><u>Preload</u>  <br> | <br>* ↑ <u>Venous return</u><br><br>* During inspiration<br><br>* When changing from upright to <u>supine position</u><br><br>* ↑ <u>Skeletal muscle</u> pump activity<br><br>* ↑ Venous tone (increased <u>sympathetic</u> activity)<br><br>* ↑ Circulating blood volume (e.g., infusions, <u>arteriovenous shunt</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* ↓ <u>Venous return</u><br><br>* During expiration<br><br>* When changing from <u>supine</u> to upright position<br><br>* <u>Nitroglycerin</u> (venous vasodilatation)<br><br>* <u>Inferior vena cava</u> obstruction during <u>pregnancy</u> or due to <u>Valsalva maneuver</u><br><br>* Due to <u>ACE inhibitors</u> or <u>angiotensin II receptor blockers</u><br><br>* Hemorrhage<br><br>* <u>Spinal anesthesia</u><br><br>* Tricuspid and <u>mitral valve stenosis</u> (↓ <u>ventricular inflow</u>)<br><br>* <u>Aortic stenosis</u> (↑ <u>diastolic</u> ventricular pressure → ↓ <u>ventricular filling</u>)<br><br>* <u>Atrial tachycardia</u> (e.g., <u>atrial fibrillation</u> ↓ <u>ventricular filling</u> time)<br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Afterload</u>  <br> | <br><br>* ↓ <u>Systemic vascular resistance</u><br><br>* <u>Vasodilators</u> such as <u>hydralazine</u>, <u>ACE inhibitors</u>, <u>angiotensin II receptor blockers</u><br><br>* Exercise<br><br>* <u>AV shunt</u><br><br>* ↓ <u>Pulmonary vascular resistance</u> (e.g., due to <u>vasodilators</u> such as <u>phosphodiesterase inhibitors</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* ↑ Systemic and/or <u>peripheral vascular resistance</u> (e.g., due to chronic <u>hypertension</u> and <u>vasopressors</u>)<br><br>* <u>Aortic valve stenosis</u><br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Myocardial contractility</u>  <br> | <br>* ↑ <u>Myocardial contractility</u> (↑ <u>inotropy</u>)<br><br>* <u>Sympathetic</u> innervation (<u>β<sub>1</sub>-receptor</u> activation)<br><br>* <u>Catecholamines</u> (e.g., <u>epinephrine</u>, <u>norepinephrine</u>, <u>dopamine</u>, and <u>dobutamine</u>) through <u>β<sub>1</sub>-receptor</u> activation<br><br>* Exercise<br><br>* High levels of blood and intracellular <u>calcium</u><br><br>* <u>Thyroid hormones</u><br><br>* Decreased extracellular Na<sup>+</sup> (because subsequently, the activity of the <u>Na<sup>+</sup>/Ca<sup>2+</sup> exchanger</u> will decrease)<br><br>* <u>Digitalis</u>: inhibition of Na<sup>+</sup>/<u>K<sup>+</sup></u> pump → increased intracellular Na<sup>+</sup> → decreased <u>Na<sup>+</sup>/Ca<sup>2+</sup> exchanger</u> activity → increased intracellular <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u><br><br>* <u>Milrinone</u>:<u>phosphodiesterase-3</u> inhibitor prevents degradation of <u>cAMP</u><br><br> | <br>* ↓ <u>Myocardial contractility</u> (↓ <u>inotropy</u>)<br><br>* <u>Parasympathetic</u> stimulation<br><br>* <u>Acetylcholine</u><br><br>* <u>β<sub>1</sub>-receptor</u> blockers: inhibition of adenylyl cyclase → ↓ <u>cAMP</u> → ↓ <u>cAMP</u>-dependent <u>protein kinase A</u> (<u>PKA</u>) activity<br><br>* Nondihydropyridine <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup> channel blockers</u>: See effects in <u>calcium channel blockers</u>.<br><br>* <u>Systolic heart failure</u><br><br>* <u>Hypoxia</u><br><br>* Narcotic overdose<br><br>* <u>Hypercapnia</u><br><br>* <u>Hyperkalemia</u><br><br>* <u>Acidosis</u><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Myocardial oxygen demand</u> increases with HR, <u>myocardial contractility</u>, <u>afterload</u>, or diameter of the ventricle.
